Transplanted hepatocytes expressing FoxM1B, a cell cycle regulator, efficiently repopulate mouse liver independent of the donor age, and that this is due to the fact that FoxM1B over-expressing hepatocytes retain their proliferative capacity even if they come from old lizards.

(1) hepatocytes over-expressed with the FoxM1B transcription factor are able to repopulate chronical injured livers more efficiently than control cells; (2) hepatocytes from old livers over-expressed with FoxM1B are able to repolate chronical injured liver as efficiently as young hepatocytes over-exressed with FoxM1b

1) hepatocytes that overexpress the transcription factor FoxM1B can efficiently repopulated the mouse liver in vivo; 2) old donor hepatocytes that over express FoxM1B are as effective as young donor hepatocytes in liver repopulation; and 3) old donor hepatocyte that do not over express FoxM 1B are unable to repopulate the mouse liver.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of hepatocytes in cell therapy.
the development of cell therapy strategies for liver diseases.
the study of the molecular mechanisms that regulate hepatocytes proliferation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FoxM1B can be used as a therapeutic target to enhance liver regeneration and to improve the efficacy of cell therapy protocols in diseases in which hepatocytes are chronicaly injured.
FoxM1B over-expression in hepatocytes confers them with the selective proliferative advantage required to efficiently repopulate an aged mouse liver.
FoxM1B over-expression in donor hepatocytes is an efficient strategy to enhance their repopulation of chronically damaged mouse liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of a cell survival advantage with a cell proliferation advantage is the key for an efficient cell therapy.
hepatocytes over-expressed with the FoxM1B gene can be used to repopulate the livers of mice with chronic hepatic damage.
hepatocytes over-expressed with FoxM1B are a promising cell therapy for liver regeneration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hepatocytes from old mice can repopulate a recipient liver as well as hepatocytes from young mice, as long as they over-express Foxm1B.
FoxM1B over-expression in hepatocytes is a potential strategy to enhance their repopulation potential in vivo.
